To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

merlin has N- and C-domain associations analogous to ERM proteins, that the merlin C-domain has a higher affinity than the N-domain for the ERM N-domain, and that the ERM C-domain inhibits EBP50 binding to the N-domain.
merlin has two domains that interact with each other and that the N-terminal domains of merlin and other ERM proteins can interact with each other.

the merlin N-terminal domain has a weak, dynamic interaction with the C-terminal domain and can bind EBP50 and that the ezrin and N-terminal merlin domains have a stronger, noncompetitive interaction that can bind both EBP50 and F-actinin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the cytoskeletal proteins ezrin, moesin, and merlin.
the regulation of the cytoskeleton and its relationship with signal transduction pathways.
the structure-function relationships of merlin and other members of the ERM protein family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
merlin is a member of the ERM family, but with a number of unique features that may be important in its role as a tumor suppressor.
ERM proteins are regulated by an intrasubunit association that is relatively weak and reversible.
ERM proteins are not just membrane cytoskeleton crosslinkers but are multifunctional proteins with roles in signal transduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

merlin is a member of the ERM protein family but that it differs from ERM proteins by having a weaker N- and C-term association and by having a lower affinity for F-actin and the scaffolding proteins E3KARP and EBP50.

the N-ERM domains of merlin and its ERM relatives bind the scaffolding proteins E3KARP and EBP50, and that these interactions are regulated by the relative affinities of these proteins for the C-ERM domains of their binding partners.
merlin and EBP50 bind to each other, and that merlin and ezrins bind to each other.
The main takeaway from our work is that

merlin is a unique ERM family member that can form oligomers and heterodimers with other ERM proteins, and this property could contribute to the regulation of merlin function and to the formation of protein complexes with other proteins.

merlin and the ERM proteins are members of an expanding family of proteins with similar structural and functional properties, and the interactions between their N- and C-domains are critical for their function and regulation
the merlin N-/C-ermad interactions are relatively weak and dynamic.
